天休命
陸大成
同考試官訓導郭　批〔古雅精純說〕〔保有意見識〕
punctuated:
人者，豈無仁義之心哉？仁必有惻隱，義必有羞惡，是惟無感，感斯通矣。豈無禮智之心哉？禮必有辭讓，智必有是非，是惟無觸，觸斯應矣。非獨先王爲然也，苟未至物欲陷溺者，皆有之。四端充足於心，不猶四體各足於身乎？非獨乍見爲然也，苟未至旦晝牿亡者，皆有之。四端具而爲人，不猶四體備而成形乎？夫使四端非人之所有，是必不出於性者也，焉有情而離性乎哉？雖然，良心人固同具，而聖凡卒至相遠者，何耶？蓋心體雖大，而其端實微。先王有之而天下運掌者，察而充也；衆人有之而自賊與賊人者，弗察而充也。他日破三品之說，復致詳焉，而乃歸于不能盡其才。噫！有才而不盡，伊誰之咎與？

易
「象曰：火在天上，大有；君子以遏惡揚善，順天休命。」
陸大成
同考試官訓導郭　批：〔古雅精純，說〕〔保有意見識。〕
translation_en:
… what is preserved in people, how could it be without a mind of benevolence and righteousness? Benevolence must have commiseration, and righteousness must have shame and dislike; only when there is no stirring is it still, for once stirred, it penetrates. How could it be without a mind of propriety and wisdom? Propriety must have modesty and complaisance, and wisdom must have approval and disapproval; only when there is no contact is it quiet, for once contacted, it responds. It is not only the former kings who were thus; anyone who has not yet been drowned by material desires possesses them. The four beginnings being fully sufficient in the mind—is this not just like the four limbs each being sufficient in the body? It is not only at a sudden sight that it is thus; anyone who has not yet had them fettered and destroyed by what they do during the day possesses them. Having the four beginnings complete so as to be a human being—is this not just like having the four limbs complete so as to form a body? Now, suppose the four beginnings were not something that people possess; then they certainly would not issue from human nature. Yet how could there be feelings that are separated from nature? Even so, the innate good mind is assuredly possessed by all alike; why then do sages and ordinary people ultimately end up so far apart from one another? It is because although the substance of the mind is great, its beginnings are in fact subtle. That the former kings possessed them and could turn the world in the palms of their hands was because they examined and expanded them; that the multitude possess them and yet injure themselves and injure others is because they fail to examine and expand them. On another day, in refuting the theory of the three grades of human nature, Mencius again explained this in detail, attributing the difference to people's inability to fully develop their native capacities. Alas! To possess such capacities and not fully develop them—whose fault is it?

Classic of Changes (Yi)
"The Commentary on the Images (Xiang) says: Fire above heaven: Great Possession (Dayou). The superior man, in accordance with this, represses evil and promotes good, and so obeys the benign mandate of Heaven."
By Lu Dacheng 陸大成.
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor (Xundao) Guo comments: [Archaic, elegant, refined, and pure; in explaining how to preserve great possession [?], it shows real insight.]

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導張　批〔發治有意明悉可誦〕
同考試官教諭范　批〔典雅剴切易義之勝者〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔雅當〕
考試官右中允高　批〔典重質雅〕
象傳申有義世有大而君子治之以天也甚矣
天命無私也君子遏惡揚善以順天而以治有
也何有哉象傳蓋謂世不常有有不常大而奉
無私以保世滋大王者之責也吾於大有得茲
義焉彼離象火也乾象天也卦唯離在乾上則
===
是天懸象而著明無私照矣火麗天而普照無
遺物矣有大之象也斯其爲大有已而君子何
以治之夫有之大可喜也亦可虞也有善而無
惡者天之休命所以�squads順之原章善而癉惡者
君之微權所以奉天之本五刑五罰不同用而
同以遏天下之惡無使反道悖德者或竊發而
滋長焉蓋天討所誅吾順而屛絶之耳而容有
一毫作惡以乖其命耶五服五章不同施而同
以揚天下之善無使廸德履道者或幽潛而末
punctuated:
同考試官訓導張　批〔發治有意，明悉可誦。〕
同考試官教諭范　批〔典雅剴切，易義之勝者。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔雅當。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔典重質雅。〕

《象傳》申有義，世有大而君子治之以天也。甚矣，天命無私也！君子遏惡揚善以順天，而以治有也，何有哉？《象傳》蓋謂：世不常有，有不常大，而奉無私以保世滋大，王者之責也。吾於《大有》得茲義焉。彼離象火也，乾象天也。卦唯離在乾上，則是天懸象而著明，無私照矣；火麗天而普照，無遺物矣。有大之象也，斯其爲《大有》已。而君子何以治之？夫有之大，可喜也，亦可虞也。有善而無惡者，天之休命，所以squads順之原；章善而癉惡者，君之微權，所以奉天之本。五刑五罰，不同用而同以遏天下之惡，無使反道悖德者或竊發而滋長焉。蓋天討所誅，吾順而屛絶之耳，而容有一毫作惡以乖其命耶？五服五章，不同施而同以揚天下之善，無使廸德履道者或幽潛而末
translation_en:
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Zhang, comments: "Expounds the meaning of governing abundance purposefully; clear, thorough, and worthy of recitation."
Associate Examiner, Instructor Fan, comments: "Classic, elegant, and incisive—a superior essay on the meaning of the Book of Changes."
Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting Luo, comments: "Elegant and fitting."
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao, comments: "Dignified, substantial, and refined."

The Commentary on the Images (Xiangzhuan) elaborates on the meaning of abundance: when the world enjoys great abundance, the superior man governs it in accordance with Heaven. Profound indeed is the impartiality of the Mandate of Heaven! When the superior man represses evil and promotes the good in order to obey Heaven, what difficulty can there be in governing abundance? The Commentary on the Images means to say that an era does not always enjoy abundance, nor is abundance always great; yet to uphold impartiality so as to preserve the world and make it flourish ever more greatly is the responsibility of the true king. We obtain this meaning from the hexagram Great Abundance (Dayou).

Now, the trigram Li symbolizes fire, and the trigram Qian symbolizes heaven. In this hexagram, because Li is above Qian, heaven suspends its images and shines forth brightly, illuminating without partiality; fire clings to heaven and shines universally, leaving nothing unlit. This is the image of possessing greatness, and thus it constitutes Great Abundance.

Yet how does the superior man govern it? Great abundance is cause for joy, yet also cause for anxiety. Possessing goodness without evil is the beneficent Mandate of Heaven, the source of compliance [?]; displaying the good and afflicting the evil is the subtle authority of the ruler, the foundation for serving Heaven. The Five Punishments and Five Fines differ in application, yet they serve alike to repress evil throughout the world, ensuring that those who violate the Way and defy virtue are never allowed to break out in secret and grow unchecked. For those whom Heaven's punishment condemns, I merely comply and cast them out—how could there be the slightest indulgence in personal malice to contravene its Mandate? The Five Robes and Five Insignia differ in bestowal, yet they serve alike to promote goodness throughout the world, ensuring that those who walk in virtue and tread the Way are never left hidden in obscurity or…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
糴焉蓋帝心所簡吾順而顯庸之耳而寧有一
毫作好以奸其命耶威福之柄擅之我而不僭
不濫聰明之實憲乎天而克類克君此君子所
以命自我出而永孚于休也使賞罰滋章而賢
否倒置逆天甚矣而能必釁孽之不萌哉吁治
有者可觀象於斯矣抑有本焉吾心之天洞若
觀火善惡消長之際而天命之逆順決矣此危
微精一之訓所以尤諄諄於帝舜也不然當紹
堯之治天下之有大矣而四凶之誅十六族之
舉何遽而能以服天下耶故曰有天德然後可
語王道信夫
===
立人之道曰仁與義
曹良貴
同考試官訓導郭　批〔說理精詳措辭溫雅〕
同考試官訓導張　批〔以心學發性命之奧明盡可式〕
同考試官教諭范　批〔渾融精潔非邃養者不能作〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔典實不浮〕
考試官右中允高　批〔潔淨雅稱易義〕
punctuated:
糴焉。蓋帝心所簡，吾順而顯庸之耳，而寧有一毫作好以奸其命耶？威福之柄擅之我而不僭不濫，聰明之實憲乎天而克類克君，此君子所以命自我出而永孚于休也。使賞罰滋章而賢否倒置，逆天甚矣，而能必釁孽之不萌哉？吁！治有者可觀象於斯矣。抑有本焉，吾心之天洞若觀火，善惡消長之際，而天命之逆順決矣。此危微精一之訓，所以尤諄諄於帝舜也。不然，當紹堯之治，天下之有大矣，而四凶之誅、十六族之舉，何遽而能以服天下耶？故曰「有天德然後可語王道」，信夫！
立人之道，曰仁與義。
曹良貴
同考試官訓導郭批：〔說理精詳，措辭溫雅。〕
同考試官訓導張批：〔以心學發性命之奧，明盡可式。〕
同考試官教諭范批：〔渾融精潔，非邃養者不能作。〕
考試官侍讀羅批：〔典實不浮。〕
考試官右中允高批：〔潔淨，雅稱易義。〕
translation_en:
…remain unadvanced [? 末糴]. For those selected by the mind of the Supreme Ancestor, I merely comply and visibly employ them; how could there be even a hair's breadth of partiality to violate His mandate? When the authority of awe and blessing is wielded by oneself without overstepping or excess, and the reality of keen hearing and clear sight is modeled upon Heaven so that one is truly discriminating and truly sovereign, this is how the noble man issues commands from himself and forever inspires trust in his beneficence. Suppose rewards and punishments were increasingly displayed while the worthy and unworthy were inverted—this would be going against Heaven in the extreme; how then could one guarantee that rifts and calamities would not sprout? Alas! Those who govern abundance in possession may observe the image here. Yet there is a root to it: when the Heaven within one's own mind is as clear as gazing at fire, at the juncture where good and evil wax and wane, compliance with or defiance of the Mandate of Heaven is decided. This is why the admonition regarding the precarious and the subtle, the refined and the unified, was especially earnest in the time of Emperor Shun. Otherwise, when succeeding to Yao's governance, the abundance possessed in the realm was already great; how could the execution of the Four Fiends and the promotion of the Sixteen Clauses so readily have brought the world to submission? Therefore it is said, "Only when one possesses Heavenly virtue can one speak of the Kingly Way." Truly it is so!

"He established the Way of Man, calling it humaneness and righteousness."
By Cao Lianggui 曹良貴.
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Guo 郭 comments: [The reasoning is precise and detailed, the phrasing gentle and elegant.]
Associate Examiner and Assistant Instructor Zhang 張 comments: [Drawing upon the Learning of the Mind, he reveals the profundities of human nature and destiny; clear and thorough, it may serve as a model.]
Associate Examiner and Instructor Fan 范 comments: [Harmonious, refined, and pure; none without deep cultivation could have composed this.]
Examiner and Reader-in-waiting Luo 羅 comments: [Substantial and classical, without superficiality.]
Examiner and Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao 高 comments: [Pure and clean, fittingly matching the meaning of the *Changes* (Yi 易).]

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
說卦論人道之所由立而知易理之原焉夫人
之有道也仁義而已矣人道之所由立不在是
哉此性命之理具於人而聖人作易之原也蓋
曰三才不同其理一也故陰陽備而天道立於
上矣剛柔備而地道立於下矣至於人也者天
生之地成之而肖形其內者不囿於器之小崇
效天卑法地而成位其中者必具乎道之全果
何以立耶曰仁與義而已蓋天之陽地之剛在
人則爲仁也天之陰地之柔在人則爲義也寛
===
裕溫柔仁足以容也而有義以裁其過心之德
與心之制合而謂人之靈於物者靈以此也發
強剛毅義足以執也而有仁以濟其偏物之宜
與物之愛協而謂人之貴於已者貴以此也繼
之者善而善非仁義不備以舒以慘之命自維
皇之降衷則然矣成之者性而性非仁義不全
克寛克嚴之德自生民之受衷則然矣蓋猶天
之有陰陽也地之有剛柔也而人之所以並立
爲三者由此道具耳借曰有仁而無義有義而
punctuated: 《說卦》論人道之所由立，而知易理之原焉。夫人之有道也，仁義而已矣。人道之所由立，不在是哉？此性命之理具於人，而聖人作《易》之原也。蓋曰：三才不同，其理一也。故陰陽備，而天道立於上矣；剛柔備，而地道立於下矣。至於人也者，天生之，地成之，而肖形其內者，不囿於器之小；崇效天，卑法地，而成位其中者，必具乎道之全。果何以立耶？曰：仁與義而已。蓋天之陽、地之剛，在人則爲仁也；天之陰、地之柔，在人則爲義也。寛裕溫柔，仁足以容也，而有義以裁其過；心之德與心之制合，而謂人之靈於物者，靈以此也。發強剛毅，義足以執也，而有仁以濟其偏；物之宜與物之愛協，而謂人之貴於已者，貴以此也。繼之者善，而善非仁義不備，以舒以慘之命，自維皇之降衷則然矣；成之者性，而性非仁義不全，克寛克嚴之德，自生民之受衷則然矣。蓋猶天之有陰陽也，地之有剛柔也，而人之所以並立爲三者，由此道具耳。借曰有仁而無義，有義而
translation_en:
The "Discussion of the Trigrams" (Shuogua) discusses that whereby the Way of Man is established, and from this we know the origin of the principles of the Changes (Yi). Now, that man possesses the Way consists of benevolence and righteousness, and nothing more. Does not that whereby the Way of Man is established lie herein? This is the principle of human nature and destiny endowed in man, and the origin of the sages' creation of the Changes. 

It says, in effect: Although the Three Powers differ, their principle is one. Therefore, when yin and yang are complete, the Way of Heaven is established above; when the firm and the yielding are complete, the Way of Earth is established below. As for man, Heaven gives him birth and Earth brings him to completion, and he who resembles their forms within them is not confined by the smallness of concrete vessels; he who emulates Heaven in its loftiness and models himself on Earth in its lowliness, thereby establishing his position in the center, must be endowed with the entirety of the Way. By what means, indeed, is it established? It is said: Benevolence and righteousness, and nothing more. 

For the yang of Heaven and the firmness of Earth, in man, become benevolence; the yin of Heaven and the yieldingness of Earth, in man, become righteousness. Broad-minded, generous, gentle, and compliant—benevolence is sufficient to be tolerant, yet there is righteousness to restrain its excesses; the virtue of the mind and the regulation of the mind unite, and when it is said that man is more intelligent than myriad things, his intelligence lies in this. Vigorous, strong, firm, and resolute—righteousness is sufficient to hold fast, yet there is benevolence to temper its partialities; what is appropriate for things and the love for things harmonize, and when it is said that man has what is noble within himself, that nobility lies in this. 

That which continues it is goodness, and goodness is not complete without benevolence and righteousness; the mandate that both unfolds in mildness and contracts in severity has been thus ever since the August Heaven sent down the moral sense. That which completes it is human nature, and human nature is not whole without benevolence and righteousness; the virtue that is capable of both leniency and strictness has been thus ever since the people received their moral sense. Indeed, it is just as Heaven has yin and yang, and Earth has the firm and the yielding; and the reason man stands alongside them as the three is simply because this Way is complete within him. Suppose it were said that there is benevolence without righteousness, or righteousness…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
無仁人道或幾乎毀矣而何以立哉性命之理
具於人蓋如此抑是仁義也對而言之則爲二
合而言之一道而已蓋道爲虛位仁與義爲定
名虛者一之神定者兩之化一不可知兩不可
執此天地之至妙也而況人乎聖人兼兩以作
易而三才之道管是矣謂易爲性命之書非哉
書
禹曰都帝慎乃在位帝曰俞
甯瑞鯉
同考試官教諭李　批〔思精詞雅發明慎位之旨警切〕
同考試官教諭潘　批〔理精調古深得君臣交儆之義〕
===
考試官侍讀羅　批〔發明懇切可式〕
考試官右中允高　批〔聖世君臣氣象宛然〕
聖君得大臣謹位之謨而然之一保治之心也
夫慎位所以保治也臣謨之而君契焉此其都
俞之盛哉且治忽有相乘之幾而君位非得肆
之地禹之孜孜固保治意也而未已也乃嘆美
而告帝曰帝位天下之至尊也亦知爲天下之
punctuated:
無仁，人道或幾乎毀矣，而何以立哉？性命之理具於人，蓋如此。抑是仁義也，對而言之則爲二，合而言之，一道而已。蓋道爲虛位，仁與義爲定名。虛者，一之神；定者，兩之化。一不可知，兩不可執，此天地之至妙也，而況人乎！聖人兼兩以作《易》，而三才之道管是矣。謂《易》爲性命之書，非哉？

《書》
「禹曰：『都！帝，慎乃在位。』帝曰：『俞。』」
甯瑞鯉
同考試官教諭李　批〔思精詞雅，發明慎位之旨，警切。〕
同考試官教諭潘　批〔理精調古，深得君臣交儆之義。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔發明懇切，可式。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔聖世君臣氣象宛然。〕

聖君得大臣謹位之謨而然之，一保治之心也。夫慎位所以保治也，臣謨之而君契焉，此其都俞之盛哉！且治忽有相乘之幾，而君位非得肆之地。禹之孜孜，固保治意也，而未已也，乃嘆美而告帝曰：帝位，天下之至尊也，亦知爲天下之
translation_en:
… without benevolence, the Way of Man would almost certainly be destroyed; how then could it be established? The principle of human nature and destiny endowed in man is indeed like this. Moreover, as for benevolence and righteousness, when spoken of in contrast, they are two; when spoken of together, they are simply one Way. For the Way is an open concept, whereas benevolence and righteousness are fixed names. What is open is the unfathomable spirit of the One; what is fixed is the transformation of the Two. The One cannot be known, and the Two cannot be rigidly grasped—this is the supreme mystery of Heaven and Earth, and how much more so for man! The sages encompassed the Two in creating the Book of Changes (Yi), and the Way of the Three Powers is governed therein. To call the Book of Changes a book of human nature and destiny—is that not right?

Book of Documents (Shu)
"Yu said, 'Oh! Emperor, be cautious on your throne.' The Emperor said, 'Yes.'"
Ning Ruili 甯瑞鯉
Associate Examiner Instructor Li 李 comments: 〔The thought is refined and the phrasing elegant; it elucidates the purport of being cautious on the throne in an admonitory and incisive manner.〕
Associate Examiner Instructor Pan 潘 comments: 〔The reasoning is precise and the tone ancient; it deeply captures the meaning of sovereign and minister mutually admonishing one another.〕
Examiner Reader-in-waiting Luo 羅 comments: 〔The elucidation is earnest and incisive; it can serve as a model.〕
Examiner Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao 高 comments: 〔Thedemeanor of sovereign and minister in a sage age is vividly rendered.〕

When a sage ruler receives a great minister's counsel on being cautious on the throne and approves it, they are united in the mind to preserve good governance. Now, being cautious on the throne is the means to preserve good governance. The minister counsels it and the ruler agrees with it—how flourishing is this harmony of "Oh!" and "Yes!" Moreover, good order and negligence have moments where they overtake one another, and the ruler's throne is no place for self-indulgence. Yu's tireless diligence was assuredly out of a desire to preserve good governance, yet he did not stop there; he therefore sighed in admiration and advised the Emperor, saying: The imperial throne is the most exalted position in the world, yet do you also know that it is the world's…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
至艱乎故必享粒食之成罔游于逸也常若懷
襄未平而不能自安于其上撫乍乂之盛罔淫
于樂也常若昏墊未復而不敢晏處乎其尊一
念不慎且有深憂守以克艱可也一日不慎且
有隱患持以儆戒可也否則君心狃于治安而
世變生于所忽能保其終哉然慎乃有位本帝
舜之心也遂答曰俞焉意以履帝位者以圖終
爲至理而論君道者以敬慎爲大原民雖粒食
矣豈其使一人肆于民上而位可逸哉汝之言
===
誠持盈之要道也可不兢業以居之耶邦雖作
乂矣豈其以一人奄有萬邦而位可樂哉汝之
言誠保泰之良規也可或怠荒以失之耶吁禹
惟愛君無已故君位已安而不忘乎矢謨帝惟
求治無窮故履位不疚而尤勤于納諫此都俞
之風不可及歟然敬脩可願舜嘗受之堯矣豈
待禹言而慎邪蓋臣恐君自足而危言儆之君
恐臣不言而虛懷契之聖世君臣之心固如此
風降而堂陛踈則有陳治安疏十漸而不終納
punctuated: 至艱乎？故必享粒食之成，罔游于逸也，常若懷襄未平，而不能自安于其上；撫乍乂之盛，罔淫于樂也，常若昏墊未復，而不敢晏處乎其尊。一念不慎，且有深憂，守以克艱可也；一日不慎，且有隱患，持以儆戒可也。否則君心狃于治安，而世變生于所忽，能保其終哉？」然慎乃有位，本帝舜之心也，遂答曰「俞」焉。意以履帝位者以圖終爲至理，而論君道者以敬慎爲大原。民雖粒食矣，豈其使一人肆于民上而位可逸哉？汝之言，誠持盈之要道也，可不兢業以居之耶？邦雖作乂矣，豈其以一人奄有萬邦而位可樂哉？汝之言，誠保泰之良規也，可或怠荒以失之耶？吁！禹惟愛君無已，故君位已安而不忘乎矢謨；帝惟求治無窮，故履位不疚而尤勤于納諫。此都俞之風不可及歟！然「敬脩可願」，舜嘗受之堯矣，豈待禹言而慎邪？蓋臣恐君自足而危言儆之，君恐臣不言而虛懷契之，聖世君臣之心固如此。風降而堂陛踈，則有陳《治安》、疏《十漸》而不終納…
translation_en:
…most arduous in the world? Therefore, even when enjoying the achievement of the people having grain to eat, one must not wander in ease; one should always feel as if the surging waters pressing upon the hills and overtopping the mounds were not yet pacified, and thus be unable to rest comfortably above them. Even when presiding over the flourishing state of newly achieved order, one must not indulge to excess in pleasure; one should always feel as if the people's distress and drowning were not yet relieved, and thus not dare to dwell leisurely in one's exalted station. If a single thought is not cautious, there will be deep sorrow—only by guarding it through overcoming difficulties will it do; if a single day is not cautious, there will be hidden perils—only by maintaining it with vigilance and warning will it do. Otherwise, if the ruler's mind grows accustomed to peace and order while worldly crises arise from what is neglected, how can he guarantee a good end?"

Yet being cautious in holding his position was originally in the heart of Emperor Shun himself, and so he replied, "Yes, indeed!" His thought was that for one who occupies the imperial throne, planning for the end is the supreme principle, and in discussing the way of the ruler, reverent caution is the great foundation. Although the people now have grain to eat, how could that allow the One Man to act without restraint above the people, as if the throne were a place for ease? Your words are truly the essential way to preserve fullness; how could I not occupy it with fear and trembling? Although the states have been brought to order, how could the One Man's possession of the myriad states make the throne a place for pleasure? Your words are truly a fine rule for preserving peace and prosperity; how could I ever lose it through negligence and indulgence?

Alas! Because Yu's love for his sovereign was unending, even when the ruler's position was already secure, he did not forget to set forth his counsels; because the Emperor's pursuit of good governance was boundless, even though he occupied the throne without fault, he was all the more diligent in accepting remonstrance. Is this not why the spirit of their "Oh!" and "Yes!" is unattainable? Yet "reverently cultivating what is desirable" was something Shun had already received from Yao; did he really need to wait for Yu's words to be cautious? It was rather that the minister feared the ruler might become self-satisfied and thus admonished him with stark words, while the ruler feared the minister might not speak and thus agreed with him with an open mind. Such was truly the mind of ruler and minister in a sage age. When customs declined and the hall and its steps grew distant, there were those who presented the Memorial on Peace and Order or submitted the Memorial on the Ten Gradual Failings, yet were not heeded to the end…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
者故人君先于虛已斯責難者不爲空言矣夫
曰皇極之敷言是彝是訓于帝其訓凡厥
庶民極之敷言是訓是行以近天子之
光曰天子作民父母以爲天下王
錢大復
同考試官教諭李　批〔天人意具見卓識而文更爽健〕
同考試官教諭潘　批〔簡潔圓融足爲崇雅之式〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔醇雅不浮〕
考試官右中允高　批〔沖粹可誦〕
===
君子著敷言之訓通乎天人者也蓋極本天人
合一之理也由同天之妙以觀感人之深而敷
言豈可已哉箕子告武王意謂人君繼天以立
極必代天以立言所以通吾心于民心者其道
繇之也吾觀皇極之敷言根乎天常而易簡得
天下之理其民秉之彝乎示乎物則而一言盡
天下之道其淑世之訓乎理曰常理則理出乎
天一帝命之有赫也訓曰大訓則言純乎天一
帝則之孔昭也敷言之妙如此皇極之君所以
punctuated:
者。故人君先于虛已，斯責難者不爲空言矣夫。

曰：「皇極之敷言，是彝是訓，于帝其訓。凡厥庶民，極之敷言，是訓是行，以近天子之光，曰：『天子作民父母，以爲天下王。』」
錢大復
同考試官教諭李　批〔天人意具見卓識，而文更爽健。〕
同考試官教諭潘　批〔簡潔圓融，足爲崇雅之式。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔醇雅不浮。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔沖粹可誦。〕

君子著敷言之訓，通乎天人者也。蓋極本天人合一之理也，由同天之妙以觀感人之深，而敷言豈可已哉？箕子告武王，意謂人君繼天以立極，必代天以立言，所以通吾心于民心者，其道繇之也。吾觀皇極之敷言，根乎天常，而易簡得天下之理，其民秉之彝乎？示乎物則，而一言盡天下之道，其淑世之訓乎？理曰常理，則理出乎天，一帝命之有赫也；訓曰大訓，則言純乎天，一帝則之孔昭也。敷言之妙如此，皇極之君所以
translation_en:
… Therefore, a ruler must first humble himself so that those who urge difficult duties upon him do not speak in vain.

"The amplification in words of the Royal Perfection is the constant norm and the instruction; it is the instruction of the Supreme Ruler. All the common people will take this amplification in words of Perfection as their instruction and put it into practice, thereby drawing near to the glory of the Son of Heaven, saying: 'The Son of Heaven is parent to the people, and thus Sovereign of All under Heaven.'" [Book of Documents, "Hongfan"]
Qian Dafu 錢大復
Associate Examiner Instructor Li 李 comments: 〔The meaning concerning Heaven and humanity shows outstanding insight, and the prose is moreover brisk and vigorous.〕
Associate Examiner Instructor Pan 潘 comments: 〔Concise and well-rounded, sufficient to serve as a model for elevating elegance.〕
Examiner Academician Reader-in-Waiting Luo 羅 comments: 〔Pure and elegant, without superficiality.〕
Examiner Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao 高 comments: 〔Modest and pure, worthy of recitation.〕

The noble man sets forth the instruction of amplified words, which penetrates both Heaven and humanity. For Ultimate Perfection is rooted in the principle of the unity of Heaven and humanity. When one observes the depth with which it moves people through the subtlety of its accord with Heaven, how could the amplification of words be dispensed with? When Jizi 箕子 addressed King Wu 武王, his meaning was that a ruler who succeeds Heaven in establishing Ultimate Perfection must speak on behalf of Heaven; the Way by which he connects his own mind with the minds of the people depends upon this. When I observe the ruler's amplification in words of the Royal Perfection, it is rooted in the constant norms of Heaven, grasping the principles of the world through ease and simplicity—is it not the invariable norm held fast by the people? It manifests the rules of things, exhausting the Way of the world in a single utterance—is it not the instruction that betters the age? When the principle is called the constant principle, it issues from Heaven, wholly as resplendent as the mandate of the Supreme Ruler; when the instruction is called the great instruction, the words are purely of Heaven, wholly as radiant as the standard of the Supreme Ruler. Such is the subtlety of amplified words; that by which the ruler of Royal Perfection…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
宣著其光輝而長育乎天下者恃有此耳而所
感何如哉凡厥庶民誦諸口者非彝訓弗道也
措諸躬者非彝訓弗履也則本至德以敷言在
天子固光昭于無外由訓行以入德在庶民亦
相近而不違蓋至是而情分之所屬者益切矣
乃頌之曰天子作民父母焉感帝訓之勤而知
生我成我者有同親也又頌之曰天子爲天下
王焉仰帝訓之嚴而知治我教我者有常尊也
會歸合而造就純錫保深而淫朋化斯皇極之
===
民也哉吁上以昭達天之妙而下以孚民心之
天信乎敷言之不容已矣大抵以人感人難以
天感人易禹謨之勸以九歌箕疇之敷以彝訓
一天之相爲感也故言易入而其化神然君心
之天乃萬化所從出者心則不純而强民以訓
無乃已踈乎日監在茲順帝之則言純心事天
也建極者尚求端焉
詩
瑟彼玉瓚黃流在中豈弟君子福祿攸降
punctuated:
宣著其光輝而長育乎天下者，恃有此耳。而所感何如哉？凡厥庶民，誦諸口者，非彝訓弗道也；措諸躬者，非彝訓弗履也。則本至德以敷言，在天子固光昭于無外；由訓行以入德，在庶民亦相近而不違。蓋至是而情分之所屬者益切矣。乃頌之曰：「天子作民父母」焉，感帝訓之勤，而知生我成我者有同親也；又頌之曰：「天子爲天下王」焉，仰帝訓之嚴，而知治我教我者有常尊也。會歸合而造就純，錫保深而淫朋化，斯皇極之民也哉！吁！上以昭達天之妙，而下以孚民心之天，信乎敷言之不容已矣。大抵以人感人難，以天感人易。《禹謨》之勸以九歌，《箕疇》之敷以彝訓，一天之相爲感也，故言易入而其化神。然君心之天，乃萬化所從出者；心則不純，而强民以訓，無乃已踈乎？「日監在茲」，「順帝之則」，言純心事天也，建極者尚求端焉。

《詩》
「瑟彼玉瓚，黃流在中。豈弟君子，福祿攸降。
translation_en:
…manifest his radiant splendor and nurture the entire world relies solely upon this. And what of the response it inspires? Among all the common people, what they recite upon their lips they will not speak unless it is this constant instruction; what they put into practice in their own persons they will not tread unless it is this constant instruction. Thus, basing himself on supreme virtue to set forth his words, the Son of Heaven shines forth with a radiance that knows no bounds; and proceeding from the practice of these instructions to enter into virtue, the common people likewise draw near to him and do not transgress. Indeed, at this point, the bonds of affection and duty that unite them become all the more intimate. Therefore they praise him, saying, "The Son of Heaven acts as father and mother to the people"—moved by the diligence of the sovereign's instruction, they recognize that he who gives them life and brings them to completion shares the same intimacy as their parents. And again they praise him, saying, "The Son of Heaven is king over all under Heaven"—looking up to the majesty of the sovereign's instruction, they recognize that he who governs and teaches them holds an enduring reverence. When their convergence and allegiance are united, their cultivation becomes pure; when the bestowal and preservation of blessings are deep, licentious factions are transformed—such, indeed, are the people of the August Ultimate! Ah! Above, it reveals the subtlety of reaching Heaven, and below, it inspires trust in the Heaven within the people's minds; truly, the setting forth of words cannot be dispensed with! On the whole, to move human beings through what is human is difficult, whereas to move human beings through Heaven is easy. The exhortation with the Nine Songs in the "Counsels of Yu" (Yu mo) and the spreading of constant instructions in the "Matrix of Jizi" (Ji chou) are both a matter of the one Heaven mutually moving hearts; therefore the words enter easily and their transformation is wondrous. Yet the Heaven within the ruler's mind is the source from which all transformations issue forth; if his mind is not pure, and yet he forces instructions upon the people, is that not wide of the mark? "Daily inspecting us here" and "following the pattern of the Lord" speak of serving Heaven with a pure mind; may he who establishes the Ultimate seek the beginning therein!

Classic of Poetry (Shi)
"Resplendent is that jade libation-ladle, with the yellow-fermented millet wine within it. Easy and self-possessed is our lord; upon him felicity and emolument descend. …

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
鳶飛戾天魚躍于淵豈弟君子遐不作
人
石崑玉
同考試官訓導李　批〔發詩旨明徹雅蔚冝寇多士〕
同考試官教諭程　批〔聖德必應之理精透融徹〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔格非詞雅迥異時作〕
同考試官教諭向　批〔天人協應正見文王之德旨哉〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔理明詞順〕
考試官右中允高　批〔詞氣敷達〕
===
詩人兩興聖德之純而天人之協應也盖德本
流通於上下者也自非豈弟之聖德烏能得天
化人之如是哉詩人咏歌之意若謂人君一身
天心視爲向背人心視爲從違而其本在德者
也吾於文王稽其盛矣彼瑟然玉瓚則黃流在
其中注寶器以珍味固物理之相須也况君子
豈弟中涵正天之所篤厚者有不足以獲福乎
但見太和默感而維皇眷祐多福壽考之駢臻
也至順潛孚而上帝寵綏明命方國之畢受也
punctuated:
鳶飛戾天，魚躍于淵。豈弟君子，遐不作人。
石崑玉
同考試官訓導李　批〔發詩旨明徹，雅蔚，冝寇多士。〕
同考試官教諭程　批〔聖德必應之理，精透融徹。〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔格非詞雅，迥異時作。〕
同考試官教諭向　批〔天人協應，正見文王之德，旨哉！〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔理明詞順。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔詞氣敷達。〕

詩人兩興聖德之純，而天人之協應也。盖德本流通於上下者也，自非豈弟之聖德，烏能得天化人之如是哉？詩人咏歌之意，若謂人君一身，天心視爲向背，人心視爲從違，而其本在德者也。吾於文王稽其盛矣。彼瑟然玉瓚，則黃流在其中，注寶器以珍味，固物理之相須也；况君子豈弟中涵，正天之所篤厚者，有不足以獲福乎？但見太和默感，而維皇眷祐，多福壽考之駢臻也；至順潛孚，而上帝寵綏，明命方國之畢受也。
translation_en:
"The hawk flies up to heaven; the fishes leap in the deep. Easy and self-possessed was our prince—did he not exert an influence upon men?"

Shi Kunyu 石崑玉
Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor (xundao) Li 李 comments: 〔It elucidates the purport of the Ode with clarity and penetration; elegant and luxuriant, it rightfully tops the multitude of scholars.〕
Associate Examiner, Instructor (jiaoyu) Cheng 程 comments: 〔The principle that sage virtue necessarily evokes a response is expounded with refined penetration and thorough mastery.〕
Associate Examiner, Instructor Zhu 朱 comments: 〔Its structure is extraordinary [?] and its diction elegant, utterly distinct from contemporary compositions.〕
Associate Examiner, Instructor Xiang 向 comments: 〔Heaven and man responding in harmony—this precisely reveals the virtue of King Wen. How profound!〕
Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting (shidu) Luo 羅 comments: 〔The reasoning is clear and the phrasing smooth.〕
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent (you zhongyun) Gao 高 comments: 〔The diction and vital breath are expansive and fluent.〕

The poet twice uses evocative imagery (xing) to celebrate the purity of sage virtue and the harmonious response of both Heaven and man. Indeed, virtue inherently circulates between above and below; were it not for an easy and self-possessed sage virtue, how could one win the favor of Heaven and transform men like this? The intent of the poet's song is as if to say: upon the single person of the ruler, the mind of Heaven looks to decide its favor or disfavor, and the minds of men look to decide their allegiance or defection—yet the root of it all lies in virtue. In King Wen I have examined this at its height. In that bright, dense jade libation-cup, the yellow fermented millet wine lies within; pouring a precious flavor into a treasured vessel is inherently the mutual dependence of the principles of things. How much more so when the prince cherishes an easy and self-possessed nature within—which is precisely what Heaven generously favors—could this be insufficient to obtain blessings? One sees only that supreme harmony silently moves above, and the August One looks down with protective grace, so that abundant blessings and longevity arrive side by side; utmost compliance secretly inspires trust, and the Lord on High bestows His favor and peace, so that the bright mandate and the states of the four quarters are all completely received. …

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
蓋雖非預爲徼福之地然以易簡之天德迓申
錫之天庥自將不期而至矣而君子何容心哉
鳶飛魚躍則戾天而在淵莘化機以自適固物
性之相忘也况君子豈弟內藴正人之所則傚
者有不足以作人乎但見中和以建極而化導
旁敷盡在野在朝而丕變也平易以近民而薰
陶覃被合有德有造而兼成也蓋雖未甞强斯
民之從然以吾心之先得感人心之同然自將
不戒而孚矣而君子何庸力哉夫一德格於上
===
下而丕應協於天人如此文王之德其可謂至
德也已矣雖然文王敢以是自足哉推其心方
且翼翼翼翼昭事而已視民如傷而已使後人能世
其執則蒼姬之曆可衍於無窮奈之何顛覆厥
德而卒貽昊天降戾無自立辟之剌也嗚呼自
古基命之主未有不本於格天導民者而守成
業者恒失之讀此詩可以知所監矣
嗟嗟臣工敬爾在公王釐爾成來咨來茹
顧龍禎
punctuated:
蓋雖非預爲徼福之地，然以易簡之天德，迓申錫之天庥，自將不期而至矣，而君子何容心哉？鳶飛魚躍，則戾天而在淵，莘化機以自適，固物性之相忘也。况君子豈弟內藴，正人之所則傚者，有不足以作人乎？但見中和以建極，而化導旁敷，盡在野在朝而丕變也；平易以近民，而薰陶覃被，合有德有造而兼成也。蓋雖未甞强斯民之從，然以吾心之先得，感人心之同然，自將不戒而孚矣，而君子何庸力哉？夫一德格於上下，而丕應協於天人如此，文王之德，其可謂至德也已矣！雖然，文王敢以是自足哉？推其心，方且翼翼翼翼昭事而已，視民如傷而已。使後人能世其執，則蒼姬之曆可衍於無窮。奈之何顛覆厥德，而卒貽「昊天降戾」、「無自立辟」之剌也！嗚呼！自古基命之主，未有不本於格天導民者，而守成業者恒失之。讀此詩，可以知所監矣。
「嗟嗟臣工，敬爾在公。王釐爾成，來咨來茹。」
顧龍禎
translation_en:
For although he did not make a point of seeking blessings in advance, yet by welcoming the repeatedly bestowed favor of Heaven with the easy and simple virtue of Heaven, those blessings would naturally arrive without being expected—so what deliberate calculation could the noble man harbor in his mind?

When the hawk flies and the fish leaps, reaching up to heaven and dwelling in the abyss, gathering [?] thevital mechanism of transformation to find their own contentment, it is inherently because the natures of creatures forget themselves in their element. How much more so when the noble man stores easygoing and brotherly virtue within—that very quality which other men take as their model and example—how could it not suffice to inspire and cultivate men? One sees only that through equilibrium and harmony he establishes the supreme standard, and his transforming guidance spreads far and wide, thoroughly changing all, whether in the wilderness or at court; through plainness and ease he draws near to the people, and his nurturing influence extends broadly, bringing both those of established virtue and those of promising talent to completion together. For although he never forced the people to follow him, yet by stirring the common disposition of human hearts with what his own heart had first attained, they would naturally be won over in trust without being admonished—so what exertion did the noble man need to use?

Now, when pure and unitary virtue reaches above and below, and the great response harmonizes Heaven and man like this, the virtue of King Wen may truly be called supreme virtue indeed! Even so, would King Wen dare to be self-satisfied with this? If we fathom his heart, he was just then ever so reverently, ever so reverently serving God brightly, and regarding the people as if they were wounded, and nothing more. Had his descendants been able to hold fast to this from generation to generation, the calendar of the house of Zhou might have been extended without end. How was it that they overturned their virtue, and in the end left behind the satirical criticisms of "Vast Heaven sends down ruin" and "Do not establish your own perverse laws" [from the Ode "Ban"]! Alas! From antiquity, among sovereigns who founded the dynastic mandate, there was never one who did not base himself upon reaching Heaven and guiding the people, whereas those who guarded the established enterprise constantly lost it. Reading this ode, one may know what to take as a mirror of warning.

"Ah, ah, ministers and officers, be reverent in your public duties! The king has given you perfect rules; come and consult, come and deliberate."

Gu Longzhen

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官訓導李　批〔詞苑意盡得周家重農之旨〕
同考試官教諭程　批〔詞語諄切發重農之意殆盡〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔發周王訓戒之意諄切可誦〕
同考試官教諭向　批〔格調典雅文詞懇切佳士也〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔渾融明爽〕
考試官右中允高　批〔頌義莊而和〕
王者戒農官以盡職亦惟王章之求而已夫人
臣必敬乃在位也而况成法有當遵者可不圖
以講求之乎昔成王以重農爲心而知農官乃
===
其專責也故進而戒之曰國家設官分職而稼
穡之政爾實司之所以重民天亦以厚國本也
嗟爾臣工尚其敬之哉無怠無荒者陳力之常
而爾以勞民勸相爲任祇慎尤所宜先也有嚴
有翼者奉公之度而爾以率作興事爲務儆惕
尤所宜切也以其身爲國家濟康阜則王事不
容以緩圖匪敬而瘝曠之咎至矣以其職爲百
姓導安養則民命不可以漫視匪敬而玩愒之
愆萌矣且今廟堂之經畫在一王有成憲焉凡
punctuated:
同考試官訓導李　批〔詞苑意盡，得周家重農之旨。〕
同考試官教諭程　批〔詞語諄切，發重農之意殆盡。〕
同考試官教諭朱　批〔發周王訓戒之意，諄切可誦。〕
同考試官教諭向　批〔格調典雅，文詞懇切，佳士也。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔渾融明爽。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔頌義莊而和。〕

王者戒農官以盡職，亦惟王章之求而已。夫人臣必敬乃在位也，而况成法有當遵者，可不圖以講求之乎？昔成王以重農爲心，而知農官乃其專責也，故進而戒之曰：「國家設官分職，而稼穡之政，爾實司之，所以重民天，亦以厚國本也。嗟爾臣工，尚其敬之哉！無怠無荒者，陳力之常，而爾以勞民勸相爲任，祇慎尤所宜先也；有嚴有翼者，奉公之度，而爾以率作興事爲務，儆惕尤所宜切也。以其身爲國家濟康阜，則王事不容以緩圖，匪敬而瘝曠之咎至矣；以其職爲百姓導安養，則民命不可以漫視，匪敬而玩愒之愆萌矣。且今廟堂之經畫，在一王有成憲焉，凡
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Assistant Instructor Li comments: [The diction is rich [?] and the meaning fully realized; it grasps the purport of the Zhou house's emphasis on agriculture.]
Associate Examiner Instructor Cheng comments: [The phrasing is earnest and incisive, bringing out the meaning of emphasizing agriculture almost exhaustively.]
Associate Examiner Instructor Zhu comments: [It brings out the meaning of the Zhou king's admonition, earnest and worthy of recitation.]
Associate Examiner Instructor Xiang comments: [The style is classic and elegant, the wording sincere and earnest—a fine scholar!]
Examiner Expositor-in-waiting Luo comments: [Harmonious, well-integrated, clear, and brisk.]
Examiner Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao comments: [The meaning of the liturgical hymn is solemn yet harmonious.]

When the true king admonishes the agricultural officials to fulfill their duties, it is simply a matter of seeking to follow the royal statutes. Now, a minister must be reverent toward his official post; how much more so when there are established laws that ought to be obeyed—can one fail to plan on investigating and seeking them out? In antiquity, King Cheng took the emphasis on agriculture to heart, and knowing that the agricultural officials held this as their specialized responsibility, he summoned them forward and admonished them, saying: "The state establishes offices and apportions duties, and the administration of sowing and reaping is truly under your charge; this is the means to honor the people's heaven [food] and also to strengthen the foundation of the state. Ah, you ministers and officers, may you be reverent in this! To be neitherremiss nor negligent is the constant norm of exerting one's strength, and since you take comforting the people and encouraging mutual aid as your responsibility, respectful caution is especially what ought to come first. To be majestic and reverent is the standard of serving the public good, and since you take leading the work and initiating affairs as your task, vigilance is especially what ought to be urgent. Because your persons bring about prosperity and abundance for the state, the king's business admits of no delayed planning; without reverence, the blame for neglecting your office will arrive. Because your offices guide the common people toward peace and nourishment, the lives of the people cannot be regarded casually; without reverence, the fault of trifling away time will sprout. Moreover, in the present planning of the court, there are established constitutions from the unified sovereign. Whenever…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
其諄諄爲猷畝言者爾當來咨之而延訪以博
其見也訓典之宣布在羣工有明賜焉凡其孳
孳爲粒食計者爾當來茹之而參度以究其故
也稟已行之紀法而曲盡夫持循之方務使無
負宵旰之慮斯已耳率不易之章程而殫效夫
考據之力務使無失小民之依斯已耳此求爾
法者正所以敬爾公也而爾可不惕然以省哉
抑人主深居九重而玉食萬方非若開創之君
躬親稼穡之艱難也乃今在廷之訓戒顧凜凜
于閭閻之憂何其勤民之切哉然必上以眞實
操法令而後下以敬畏奉法守否則日懸象魏
而申飭之猶空文也願治者其審諸
===
春秋
夏六月公會齊侯宋公陳侯鄭伯同盟于
幽〔莊公二十有七年〕六月公會宋公陳
侯衛侯鄭伯許男曹伯晉趙盾癸酉同
盟于新城〔文公十有四年〕
史懋文
punctuated:
其諄諄爲猷畝言者，爾當來咨之，而延訪以博其見也；訓典之宣布，在羣工有明賜焉，凡其孳孳爲粒食計者，爾當來茹之，而參度以究其故也。稟已行之紀法，而曲盡夫持循之方，務使無負宵旰之慮，斯已耳；率不易之章程，而殫效夫考據之力，務使無失小民之依，斯已耳。此求爾法者，正所以敬爾公也，而爾可不惕然以省哉？抑人主深居九重，而玉食萬方，非若開創之君躬親稼穡之艱難也。乃今在廷之訓戒，顧凜凜于閭閻之憂，何其勤民之切哉！然必上以眞實操法令，而後下以敬畏奉法守，否則日懸象魏而申飭之，猶空文也。願治者其審諸！」

《春秋》
「夏六月，公會齊侯、宋公、陳侯、鄭伯同盟于幽。」〔莊公二十有七年〕「六月，公會宋公、陳侯、衛侯、鄭伯、許男、曹伯、晉趙盾，癸酉，同盟于新城。」〔文公十有四年〕
史懋文
translation_en:
…all those earnest words spoken on behalf of the farmed fields—you must come to consult them and make wide inquiries to broaden your view; in the promulgation of instructive canons, the assembled officials have been granted clear guidance, so all those diligent plans made for the people's grain food—you must come to weigh them and deliberate comparatively to get to the bottom of their rationale. Receive the established laws and regulations already in force and exhaustively carry out the means of upholding and following them, striving only not to fail the sovereign's anxious thoughts from before dawn until late at night; follow the immutable statutes and rules and devote your utmost strength to examining and verifying them, striving only not to lose that upon which the common people depend. That I require you to seek out the models in this way is precisely how you are to reverently attend to your public duty—and can you fail to examine yourselves with vigilance?"

Yet a ruler dwells deep within the ninefold palace walls and dines on the finest fare of the myriad regions; he is not like a founding monarch who personally experienced the hardships of sowing and reaping. That today the admonitions issued at court nevertheless tremble with concern for the sorrows of the village lanes—how earnest is this diligence on behalf of the people! Even so, only when those above wield laws and ordinances with genuine sincerity will those below uphold their legal duties with reverent awe; otherwise, though one hang them daily from the palace gates and repeatedly enjoin them, they remain mere empty words. May those who desire good governance examine this well!

Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu)

"In summer, in the sixth month, the Duke met the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng, and together they made a covenant at You." [27th year of Duke Zhuang] "In the sixth month, the Duke met the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Baron of Xu, the Earl of Cao, and Zhao Dun of Jin; on the guiyou day, together they made a covenant at Xincheng." [14th year of Duke Wen]

Shi Maowen 史懋文

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官推官舒　批〔義正辭嚴最得聖人尊王之旨〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔嚴整可式〕
考試官右中允高　批〔發書同意殆盡〕
二伯協尊攘之信經皆志其同欲也此見春秋
不可無伯亦不可無從伯之諸侯于幽新城之
盟君子爲世道幸矣蓋昔黍離之賦天下傷之
自伯圖肇興王綱攸賴聖人於會盟離合之間
每致意焉是故我莊之世創伯者齊也維時侯
度無統東向之轅未堅伯業其難以濟矣乃今
===
之盟于幽也安攘之勢既成觀望之情漸一雖
反覆如鄭亦受盟壇坫而帖然聽命之不遑焉
即一鄭而衆志可知已北杏倡會以來茲非其
獨盛者哉噫夾輔之風邈矣修世勳以獎王室
微齊桓將誰與歸也則多助之人心豈其所可
少者經故特書曰同幸諸侯之從齊耳我文之
世嗣伯者晉也維時晉君方少北圖之釁日啟
中國且胥爲夷矣乃今之盟新城也推戴之念
惟均攘郤之謀允協雖從楚如三國亦承奉齊
punctuated:
同考試官推官舒　批〔義正辭嚴，最得聖人尊王之旨。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔嚴整可式。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔發「書同」意殆盡。〕
二伯協尊攘之信，經皆志其同欲也。此見春秋不可無伯，亦不可無從伯之諸侯。于幽、新城之盟，君子爲世道幸矣。蓋昔《黍離》之賦，天下傷之。自伯圖肇興，王綱攸賴，聖人於會盟離合之間，每致意焉。是故我莊之世，創伯者齊也。維時侯度無統，東向之轅未堅，伯業其難以濟矣。乃今之盟于幽也，安攘之勢既成，觀望之情漸一；雖反覆如鄭，亦受盟壇坫，而帖然聽命之不遑焉。即一鄭而衆志可知已。北杏倡會以來，茲非其獨盛者哉！噫！夾輔之風邈矣，修世勳以獎王室，微齊桓將誰與歸也？則多助之人心，豈其所可少者？經故特書曰「同」，幸諸侯之從齊耳。我文之世，嗣伯者晉也。維時晉君方少，北圖之釁日啟，中國且胥爲夷矣。乃今之盟新城也，推戴之念惟均，攘郤之謀允協；雖從楚如三國，亦承奉齊…
translation_en:
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Shu, comments: 〔The principle is upright and the diction stern; it best captures the Sage's intent of honoring the King.〕
Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting Luo, comments: 〔Strict and well-ordered, worthy of serving as a model.〕
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao, comments: 〔It almost completely exhausts the meaning of why the word "jointly" (tong) was recorded.〕

When the two hegemons brought harmony to the covenant of honoring the King and repelling the barbarians, the Classic in both cases recorded that they shared the same desire. From this we see that the Spring and Autumn period could not do without hegemons, nor could it do without feudal lords who followed the hegemons. In the covenants at You and Xincheng, the gentleman rejoiced for the state of the world. In the past, when the ode "Millet Lush" (Shuli) was composed, all under Heaven grieved over it. Once hegemonic enterprises began to rise, the royal order had something to rely upon, and the Sage always paid close attention to the comings together and partings in meetings and covenants.

Therefore, in the era of our Duke Zhuang, the one who founded the hegemony was Qi. At that time, the conduct of the feudal lords lacked unity, the chariot shafts turned eastward toward Qi were not yet steadfast, and the hegemonic enterprise was difficult to bring to success. Yet now, in the covenant at You, the momentum for pacifying the interior and repelling the exterior had already taken shape, and those who had been hesitantly watching gradually became united in sentiment. Even a state as capricious as Zheng accepted the covenant at the altar and mound, submissively obeying orders without a moment's delay. From the single case of Zheng, the will of the multitude can be known! Since Qi first initiated the assembly at Beixing, was this not uniquely flourishing? Alas! The ancient custom of flanking and assisting the royal house was already distant. To cultivate hereditary merit in order to support the royal house—if not for Duke Huan of Qi, to whom could one turn? How then could the popular support that brings abundant aid be dispensed with? The Classic therefore specially writes "jointly," rejoicing that the feudal lords followed Qi.

In the era of our Duke Wen, the one who succeeded to the hegemony was Jin. At that time, the ruler of Jin was still young, rifts from the southern power's northward designs were opening daily, and the Central States were on the verge of all turning into barbarians. Yet now, in the covenant at Xincheng, the thought of upholding the leader was shared by all alike, and the plans for repelling the enemy were truly in harmony. Even the three states that had followed Chu respectfully offered the sacrificial…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
犧而憣然改圖之恐後焉卽三國而衆志可知
已于扈要盟以來玆不爲循愈乎哉噫糾逖之
功遐矣振先烈以翼宗周于晉靈尚有厚望也
則偕好之友邦亦足倚爲重者經故特書曰同
幸諸侯之從晉耳夫聖人於齊晉奚私哉蓋爲
周室慮至惓惓也然自此而伐楚封衛一介不
遺桓亦幾於改物矣楚之爭鄭憑華竟與晉靈
之伯相爲終始同盟之諸侯將安用之嗟乎伯
業盛則天下以空名事王伯業衰則天下以空
名事伯亦其勢然也故春秋不得已而予齊桓
冬十月公會晉侯宋公衛侯鄭伯曹伯莒
子邾子滕子薛伯杞伯小邾子同圍齊
襄公十有八年公至自伐齊襄公十有
九年
===
湯以栢
同考試官推官舒　批〔發春秋抑强之意明盡可錄〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔詞旨嚴正〕
考試官右中允高　批〔專核詞直〕
punctuated:
犧而憣然改圖之恐後焉。卽三國而衆志可知已。于扈要盟以來，玆不爲循愈乎哉？噫！糾逖之功遐矣，振先烈以翼宗周，于晉靈尚有厚望也，則偕好之友邦，亦足倚爲重者。經故特書曰「同」，幸諸侯之從晉耳。夫聖人於齊、晉奚私哉？蓋爲周室慮至惓惓也。然自此而伐楚、封衛，一介不遺，桓亦幾於改物矣；楚之爭鄭、憑華，竟與晉靈之伯相爲終始，同盟之諸侯將安用之？嗟乎！伯業盛，則天下以空名事王；伯業衰，則天下以空名事伯，亦其勢然也。故《春秋》不得已而予齊桓。

冬十月，公會晉侯、宋公、衛侯、鄭伯、曹伯、莒子、邾子、滕子、薛伯、杞伯、小邾子同圍齊〔襄公十有八年〕。公至自伐齊〔襄公十有九年〕。

湯以栢
同考試官推官舒　批〔發《春秋》抑强之意，明盡可錄。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔詞旨嚴正。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔專核詞直。〕
translation_en:
…the sacrificial victim and suddenly changed their plans, fearing only to be left behind. From those three states alone, the will of all can be known. Since the coerced covenant at Hu, was this not decidedly better [?]? Alas! The merit of uniting those far away was now distant; to revive ancestral achievements and shelter the royal house of Zhou, great hopes were still placed in Duke Ling of Jin, and thus the friendly states that joined in amity could also be relied upon for weight. The Classic therefore specially records the word "together" (tong), rejoicing that the feudal lords followed Jin. Now, what private partiality did the Sage have toward Qi or Jin? Indeed, his concern for the house of Zhou was utmost and earnest. Yet after this, in attacking Chu and enfeoffing Wei, not even a single envoy was dispatched to the King, so Duke Huan came close to altering the royal prerogatives; and Chu's contention over Zheng and encroachment upon the Central States ultimately lasted from the beginning to the end of Duke Ling of Jin's hegemony—what use then were the feudal lords of the common covenant? Alas! When the霸業 (hegemonic enterprise) flourished, the realm served the King as an empty name; when the hegemonic enterprise declined, the realm served the Hegemon as an empty name—such was the inevitable trend of circumstances. Therefore, only out of necessity did the Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) grant approval to Duke Huan of Qi.

"In winter, in the tenth month, the Duke met with the Marquis of Jin, the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Wei, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, the Viscount of Ju, the Viscount of Zhu, the Viscount of Teng, the Earl of Xue, the Earl of Qi, and the Viscount of Little Zhu, and together they besieged Qi" [18th year of Duke Xiang]. "The Duke arrived from the campaign against Qi" [19th year of Duke Xiang].

Tang Yibai.
Associate Examiner, Prefectural Judge Shu, comments: [It brings out the Spring and Autumn Annals' intent of curbing the strong; clear and thorough, worthy of selection.]
Examiner, Academician Reader-in-Waiting Luo, comments: [The diction and purport are stern and upright.]
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao, comments: [Focused and incisive, with forthright language.]

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
春秋曲全諸侯討罪之兵而受兵者之惡著矣
夫國必自伐而後人伐之春秋之罪齊也亦抑
强暴之意與自魯濟有會圍齊之兵所爲合也
逮乎泝上還師而我公告至焉夫合黨凌人非
春秋所禁乎而奚以罪齊葢聞之曰君子無始
禍無怙亂禍福之至靡弗自已求之者列國之
圍齊豈無故而加之兵哉良由齊也棄盟好而
日尋干戈肆凌虐而數伐隣國其稔惡非一朝
夕矣以故佳兵好還出爾有反爾之報重怒難
===
任不戢有自焚之災圻父之歌鴻鴈之賦仇齊
者一魯耳乃同仇之義槩翕然不戒以自孚涉
河而誓沉玉而禱首事者一晉耳乃共事之人
心羣然不謀而自協平陰入而二臣獲齊之禍
深矣而其受之也非不幸雍門次而四郭焚諸
侯之憤洩矣而其加之也非爲暴何者今而後
得反之也向使齊無可加之釁則世胙大師股
肱之烈未泯纂乃祖考天王之命方新晉魯諸
國相率而親睦之恐後奚至剪爲仇讐若此哉
punctuated: 《春秋》曲全諸侯討罪之兵，而受兵者之惡著矣。夫國必自伐而後人伐之，《春秋》之罪齊也，亦抑强暴之意與？自魯濟有會，圍齊之兵所爲合也；逮乎泝上還師，而我公告至焉。夫合黨凌人，非《春秋》所禁乎？而奚以罪齊？葢聞之曰：「君子無始禍，無怙亂。」禍福之至，靡弗自已求之者。列國之圍齊，豈無故而加之兵哉？良由齊也，棄盟好而日尋干戈，肆凌虐而數伐隣國，其稔惡非一朝夕矣。以故佳兵好還，出爾有反爾之報；重怒難任，不戢有自焚之災。「圻父」之歌、「鴻鴈」之賦，仇齊者一魯耳，乃同仇之義，槩翕然不戒以自孚；涉河而誓，沉玉而禱，首事者一晉耳，乃共事之人心，羣然不謀而自協。平陰入而二臣獲，齊之禍深矣，而其受之也非不幸；雍門次而四郭焚，諸侯之憤洩矣，而其加之也非爲暴。何者？今而後得反之也。向使齊無可加之釁，則世胙大師，股肱之烈未泯；纂乃祖考，天王之命方新。晉、魯諸國相率而親睦之恐後，奚至剪爲仇讐若此哉？
translation_en:
The Spring and Autumn Annals (Chunqiu) goes out of its way to justify the punitive expedition of the feudal lords, and thus the wickedness of the target of that expedition is made manifest. Indeed, a state must first strike itself before others will strike it; in condemning Qi, does not the Spring and Autumn Annals also express the intent of suppressing the strong and violent?

With the meeting at the Ji River in Lu, the troops for the siege of Qi were brought together; when the army returned from the Su River, our Duke reported his arrival back at the ancestral temple. Now, is not forming factions to bully others something forbidden by the Spring and Autumn Annals? Why, then, does it condemn Qi?

It is heard that "the superior man does not initiate calamity, nor does he rely on disorder." Whether misfortune or blessing arrives, there is none that is not brought upon oneself. When the various states besieged Qi, how could they have inflicted arms upon it without cause? It was truly because Qi had abandoned covenant friendships and daily resorted to weapons of war, indulging in bullying and cruelty and repeatedly attacking neighboring states—its accumulated evils were not the work of a single morning or evening. Therefore, fine weapons are fond of rebounding, and what goes out from you returns to you in retribution; heavy wrath is difficult to bear, and failure to lay down arms brings the disaster of burning oneself.

When "Royal Commander" (Qifu) was sung and "Wild Geese" (Hongyan) was recited, the one harboring enmity toward Qi was Lu alone; yet in the righteousness of shared enmity, all united harmoniously and trusted one another without prior warning. When crossing the Yellow River to swear an oath and sinking jade to pray, the one initiating the campaign was Jin alone; yet the hearts of those sharing in the enterprise all came into accord without prior consultation. When Pingyin was entered and two ministers were captured, Qi's calamity was deep indeed, yet its suffering this was no mere misfortune; when the army encamped at the Yong Gate and the four outer walls were burned, the indignation of the feudal lords was vented, yet their inflicting this was not an act of tyranny. Why is this? Because only from this moment on were they able to pay Qi back.

Had Qi given no provocation inviting attack, then since it had been hereditarily enfeoffed as Grand Preceptor, the illustrious merit of its service as the royal right-hand would not have been extinguished; and having succeeded to its ancestors, the charge from the Heavenly King would have been freshly renewed. The states of Jin, Lu, and the others would have led one another to cultivate amity with it for fear of being left behind—how would they have come to cut it off as a mortal enemy like this?

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
經故書同圍齊以見其公書公至自伐齊以大
其事圍齊者無罪則見伐者之惡豈容掩哉雖
然晉亦未爲得也自于溫之宴歌詩弗類荀偃
一怒而高厚逃歸晉之欲甘心于齊舊矣故特
假鳩魯之名以逞其私而主之者則又荀偃也
天討之義馭下之權兩者胥失焉晉伯之日趨
於不兢也宜哉
禮記
是故清明象天廣大象地終始象四時周
===
還象風雨五色成文而不亂八風從律
而不姦百度得數而有常小大相成終
始相生倡和清濁迭相爲經
閻士選
同考試官教諭曾　批〔冲雅明瑩檃括得體〕〔宜録之〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔說理融洽〕
考試官右中允高　批〔綣節中有條貫〕
論大樂之作極其法之善焉蓋先王作樂之有
方也準造化而兼常變其法之善何如哉樂記
punctuated:
《經》故書「同圍齊」，以見其公；書「公至自伐齊」，以大其事。圍齊者無罪，則見伐者之惡，豈容掩哉？雖然，晉亦未爲得也。自于溫之宴，歌詩弗類，荀偃一怒而高厚逃歸，晉之欲甘心于齊，舊矣。故特假鳩魯之名以逞其私，而主之者則又荀偃也。天討之義、馭下之權，兩者胥失焉。晉伯之日趨於不兢也，宜哉！

《禮記》：「是故清明象天，廣大象地，終始象四時，周還象風雨。五色成文而不亂，八風從律而不姦，百度得數而有常。小大相成，終始相生。倡和清濁，迭相爲經。」

閻士選
同考試官教諭曾　批〔冲雅明瑩，檃括得體，宜録之。〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔說理融洽。〕
考試官右中允高　批〔綣節中有條貫。〕

論大樂之作，極其法之善焉。蓋先王作樂之有方也，準造化而兼常變，其法之善何如哉？《樂記》
translation_en:
The Classic [Spring and Autumn Annals] therefore records that they "jointly besieged Qi" to show the public-spiritedness of the act, and records that "the Duke arrived from attacking Qi" to magnify the affair. Since those who besieged Qi were blameless, how could the wickedness of the one who was attacked be concealed? Even so, Jin cannot be considered to have acted rightly either. Ever since the banquet at Wen, when the poem sung was inappropriate, Xun Yan 荀偃 flew into a rage and Gao Hou 高厚 fled home, Jin had long wished to vent its spleen upon Qi. Therefore it merely borrowed the pretext of giving relief to Lu in order to indulge its own private grievance, and the one who directed the affair was moreover Xun Yan. The righteousness of Heaven's punishment and the authority to control one's subordinates were both lost in this. That Jin's hegemony daily declined into weakness was only fitting!

Record of Rites (Liji): "Therefore, in its clear brightness it models itself on heaven; in its broad vastness it models itself on earth; in its endings and beginnings it models itself on the four seasons; in its revolutions it models itself on the wind and rain. The five colors form a pattern without confusion; the eight winds follow the pitch-tubes without disorder; the hundred measures attain their proper numbers and remain constant. Small and great complete one another; ending and beginning give rise to one another. Leading and responding, clear and turbid tones alternate with one another as the warp."

Yan Shixuan 閻士選
Associate Examiner, Instructor Zeng 曾, comments: "Modest, refined, bright, and lucid; it summarizes and structures the material appropriately. It ought to be recorded [for publication]."
Examiner, Academician Reader-in-waiting Luo 羅, comments: "The exposition of principle is harmonious and thorough."
Examiner, Right Companion to the Heir Apparent Gao 高, comments: "Within a compact structure [?] there is a coherent thread."

When discussing the creation of great music, it carries the perfection of its method to the utmost. Indeed, the former kings had a proper method in creating music: taking nature's creative transformations as their standard and encompassing both constancy and change, how admirable was the perfection of their method! The "Record of Music" (Yueji)…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
若謂先王之樂會本文之全昭功用之大樂之
所觀者深矣抑知其作之盡善乎是故天以清
明之氣上浮而樂有聲皆氣之爲也其皦然清
明者崇則效乎天地以廣大之質下凝而樂有
體皆質之具也其熙然廣大者卑則法乎地終
始運而樂之條理生矣則與四時之推遷者合
其序周還交而樂之變化見矣則與風雨之散
潤者符其節樂法造化如此其妙豈一端所能
盡哉語乎其常五聲配五行之色節奏合以成
===
文而何亂八音配八卦之風氣候協以從律而
何姦度出於律數起於度由一度之衍至百度
之繁參兩之而倚數也又何失其常乎語乎其
變以律小大而宮羽之稱交錯以相成以比終
始而鍾呂之序循環以相生倡和生於變清濁
從乎體以清濁之聲主倡和之應纍纍乎如貫
珠也又非迭相爲經乎吁樂法造化則達之常
變而自宜樂兼常變則參之造化而愈合由是
而效之獲也夫豈強致哉抑此特制作之迹耳
punctuated: 若謂：先王之樂，會本文之全，昭功用之大，樂之所觀者深矣；抑知其作之盡善乎？是故天以清明之氣上浮，而樂有聲，皆氣之爲也，其皦然清明者崇，則效乎天；地以廣大之質下凝，而樂有體，皆質之具也，其熙然廣大者卑，則法乎地。終始運而樂之條理生矣，則與四時之推遷者合其序；周還交而樂之變化見矣，則與風雨之散潤者符其節。樂法造化如此，其妙豈一端所能盡哉？語乎其常，五聲配五行之色，節奏合以成文，而何亂？八音配八卦之風，氣候協以從律，而何姦？度出於律，數起於度，由一度之衍至百度之繁，參兩之而倚數也，又何失其常乎？語乎其變，以律小大，而宮羽之稱交錯以相成；以比終始，而鍾呂之序循環以相生。倡和生於變，清濁從乎體，以清濁之聲主倡和之應，纍纍乎如貫珠也，又非迭相爲經乎？吁！樂法造化，則達之常變而自宜；樂兼常變，則參之造化而愈合。由是而效之獲也，夫豈強致哉？抑此特制作之迹耳。
translation_en: …seems to say: The music of the former kings brings together the completeness of substance and refinement, and makes manifest the greatness of its functional efficacy; what may be observed in music is profound indeed! Yet do we also recognize how utterly perfected its creation was? Therefore, Heaven with its clear and bright vital energy floats upward, and since music has sound—all of which is the work of vital energy—that in it which is brilliantly clear and bright is exalted, thus modeling itself upon Heaven. Earth with its vast and great material substance condenses below, and since music has form—all of which is the embodiment of substance—that in it which is serenely vast and great is lowly, thus patterning itself upon Earth. As end and beginning revolve, the orderly progression of music is generated, matching in sequence the succession of the four seasons; as circling movements interlock, the transformations of music appear, tallying in rhythm with the dispersing and moistening of wind and rain. Since music patterns itself upon the creative forces of nature in this way, how could its marvels be exhausted by any single aspect? Speaking of its constancy: the five tones correspond to the five colors of the Five Phases, their rhythms and cadences combining to form a pattern—so how could they fall into disorder? The eight timbres correspond to the winds of the Eight Trigrams, their seasonal breaths harmonizing to follow the pitch-pipes—so how could they become licentious? Measures issue from the pitch-pipes, and numbers arise from measures; from the extension of a single measure to the multiplicity of the hundred measures, they are combined by threes and twos to establish numerical proportions—so how could they ever lose their constancy? Speaking of its transformations: when measured by small and great, the designations of the gong and yu notes interweave to complete one another; when arrayed from end to beginning, the sequence of the yang and yin pitch-pipes circulates to generate one another. Leading and responding arise from transformation, while clear and turbid tones follow from material form; using clear and turbid sounds to govern the resonance of leading and responding, linked together like a string of pearls—is this not taking turns as the guiding warp? Ah! Because music patterns itself upon the creative forces of nature, when extended through constancy and transformation it is naturally fitting; because music encompasses both constancy and transformation, when aligned with the creative forces of nature it accords all the more closely. That its effects are thereby achieved—how could this be brought about by force? Yet all of this is merely the outward trace of its creation…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
要之樂以章德德盛而樂斯備也君子反情比
類預立乎樂之本而後器數從之則始焉法造
化終且賛乎造化而體常盡變之間無非裁成
輔相之用矣否則將如樂何而矧於功化之妙
乎是故不聞性與天道而欲議樂者末也
孔子曰安上治民莫善於禮此之謂也
吳　棐
同考試官教諭曾　批〔發明安治之義古雅無一長語〕
考試官侍讀羅　批〔典雅明暢〕
===
考試官右中允高　批〔文亦典確〕
觀聖人之言則知禮之爲用大矣夫禮者物之
致也由聖言觀之則其用之大不益明乎且夫
敬讓行而達之無往不順禮誠軌世之善物也
而非無徵也昔孔子嘗曰安上治民莫善於禮
蓋言上之道揆雖非一然有禮則安而藏身之
固庸禮之外無他事也下之法守雖非一然得
禮則治而民分之定達禮之餘無多術也孔子
之言如此其斯敬讓盡道而無入不得之謂乎
punctuated:
要之，樂以章德，德盛而樂斯備也。君子反情比類，預立乎樂之本，而後器數從之。則始焉法造化，終且賛乎造化，而體常盡變之間，無非裁成輔相之用矣。否則，將如樂何？而矧於功化之妙乎！是故不聞性與天道，而欲議樂者，末也。
孔子曰：「安上治民，莫善於禮。」此之謂也。
吳棐
同考試官教諭曾批〔發明安治之義，古雅無一長語。〕
考試官侍讀羅批〔典雅明暢。〕
考試官右中允高批〔文亦典確。〕
觀聖人之言，則知禮之爲用大矣。夫禮者，物之致也；由聖言觀之，則其用之大，不益明乎？且夫敬讓行而達之無往不順，禮誠軌世之善物也，而非無徵也。昔孔子嘗曰：「安上治民，莫善於禮。」蓋言上之道揆雖非一，然有禮則安，而藏身之固，庸禮之外無他事也；下之法守雖非一，然得禮則治，而民分之定，達禮之餘無多術也。孔子之言如此，其斯敬讓盡道而無入不得之謂乎！
translation_en:
In short, music serves to manifest virtue; when virtue is abundant, music is thereby complete. The gentleman returns to true feelings and compares categories, establishing in advance the foundation of music, and only afterward do the instruments and numerical measures follow it. Thus, in the beginning one models oneself on the creative transformations of nature, and in the end one even assists those creative transformations; and between embodying the constant and exhausting the variable, there is nothing that is not the function of regulating and assisting nature! Otherwise, what can one do with music—and how much less with the subtleties of its meritorious transformations! Therefore, to wish to discuss music without having heard of human nature and the Way of Heaven is to attend only to the branches.

"Confucius said: 'For securing the rulers above and governing the people below, there is nothing better than ritual propriety.' This is what is meant."
Wu Fei 吳棐
Associate Examiner Instructor Zeng 曾 comments: [He elucidates the meaning of securing and governing; it is antique and elegant, without a single superfluous word.]
Examiner Academician Reader-in-waiting Luo 羅 comments: [Classical, elegant, clear, and fluent.]
Examiner Right Companion of the Heir Apparent Gao 高 comments: [The writing is also classical and precise.]

When we observe the words of the Sage, we know that the function of ritual propriety is great indeed. Now, ritual propriety is the ultimate standard of things; when we observe it through the Sage's words, is not the greatness of its function all the more evident? Moreover, when reverence and deference are practiced and extended, there is nowhere one goes that is not harmonious. Ritual propriety is truly an excellent thing for regulating the world, and this is not without proof. In the past, Confucius once said: "For securing the rulers above and governing the people below, there is nothing better than ritual propriety." This means that although the guiding principles of those above are not unitary, when they possess ritual propriety they are secure, and for the firmness of safeguarding their own persons, there is no other business outside of practicing constant ritual propriety; and although the laws and observances of those below are not unitary, when they attain ritual propriety they are well-governed, and for the settling of the people's lot, there are not many techniques beyond extending ritual propriety. Since the words of Confucius are like this, is this not what is meant by reverence and deference exhausting the Way, so that nowhere one enters is not fitting?

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
夫自孔子言之若謂禮之切於上下云爾然禮
者嘉之會也由上下推之是故無物而不在禮
矣謂禮之繫於治安云爾然禮者衆之紀也由
治安推之是故禮周流無不徧矣宗廟朝廷上
下寓焉敬讓以行此而在廟極敬在朝極辨所
以通乎幽明之交者何安且治也然則孔子之
極言禮也非此之謂與室家鄉里上下寓焉敬
讓以行此而內和於室外理於鄉所以稱乎親
疏之情者何安且治也然則我之聞禮於孔子
===
也非此之謂與夫上以禮安則爲上而不知謹
禮者非也民以禮治則爲民而不知守禮者亦
非也然則隆由之功其可或已哉大抵治安之
善信莫如禮乃其道之所繇者何噫言之矣不
曰修已以敬而安人乎不曰以禮讓爲國乎惟
敬則篤恭之治神讓則太和之化洽此體信達
順之功唐虞三代之極致也獨有方士乎哉然
語聖學之要則尤在主敬秉禮者尚懋懋諸
第貳場
punctuated:
夫自孔子言之，若謂禮之切於上下云爾。然禮者，嘉之會也。由上下推之，是故無物而不在禮矣。謂禮之繫於治安云爾，然禮者，衆之紀也。由治安推之，是故禮周流無不徧矣。宗廟、朝廷，上下寓焉，敬讓以行此，而在廟極敬，在朝極辨，所以通乎幽明之交者，何安且治也！然則孔子之極言禮也，非此之謂與？室家、鄉里，上下寓焉，敬讓以行此，而內和於室，外理於鄉，所以稱乎親疏之情者，何安且治也！然則我之聞禮於孔子也，非此之謂與？夫上以禮安，則爲上而不知謹禮者非也；民以禮治，則爲民而不知守禮者亦非也。然則隆由之功，其可或已哉？大抵治安之善，信莫如禮。乃其道之所繇者何？噫，言之矣！不曰「修已以敬」而「安人」乎？不曰「以禮讓爲國」乎？惟敬則篤恭之治神，讓則太和之化洽。此體信達順之功，唐虞三代之極致也，獨有方士乎哉？然語聖學之要，則尤在主敬。秉禮者尚懋懋諸！

第貳場
translation_en:
Now, judging from Confucius's words, it is as though he said merely that ritual propriety is pertinent to superiors and inferiors. Yet ritual propriety is the convergence of all excellence; extending this from superiors and inferiors, there is therefore nothing that does not reside within ritual propriety. It is as though he said merely that ritual propriety is bound up with order and security. Yet ritual propriety is the regulating thread of the multitude; extending this from order and security, ritual propriety therefore circulates everywhere without omission. In the ancestral temple and the royal court, the distinction between superior and inferior is embodied; when reverence and deference are practiced therein, there is utmost reverence in the temple and utmost discernment of rank at court—how secure and well-ordered is that which mediates the intercourse between the unseen spirits and the visible world! If so, when Confucius spoke in the highest terms of ritual propriety, was it not this that he meant? In the family household and the village community, the distinction between superior and inferior is embodied; when reverence and deference are practiced therein, there is harmony within the household and order outside in the village—how secure and well-ordered is that which matches the feelings of intimacy and distance! If so, what I have heard of ritual propriety from Confucius, is it not this that was meant? Now, since superiors are made secure through ritual propriety, to be a superior and not know to be circumspect in ritual propriety is wrong; since the common people are governed through ritual propriety, to be among the common people and not know to abide by ritual propriety is likewise wrong. How, then, could the effort of exalting and following ritual propriety ever cease? On the whole, for the perfection of order and security, truly nothing surpasses ritual propriety. Yet whence does its Way originate? Ah, it has already been stated! Was it not said, "Cultivate oneself with reverence" so as to "bring security to others"? Was it not said, "Govern a state through ritual propriety and deference"? Only through reverence does the governance of steadfast respect become numinous, and through deference does the transforming influence of supreme harmony pervade all. This achievement of embodying sincerity and attaining compliance was the ultimate perfection of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties—was it unique to a single state's scholars [?]? Yet in speaking of the essentials of sagely learning, it lies above all in making reverence one's master. May those who uphold ritual propriety exert themselves to the utmost in this!

Second Session

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
論
人主恭已於上　石崑玉
同考試官訓導李　批〔詞古意盡末重主敬親賢尤切要之論宜錄之以式多士〕
同考試官教諭程　批〔議論古雅才識宏邃發明恭已之由在信任宰執臺諫剴切明盡而末復歸之主敬親賢只足占忠愛矣〕

"The Ruler Maintains Reverent Self-Cultivation on High" — Shi Kunyu 石崑玉

Associate Examiner, Assistant Instructor Li 李, comments: [The diction is archaic and the meaning exhaustive. At the end, it emphasizes holding fast to reverence and drawing close to the worthy—an especially incisive and essential discourse. It should be recorded as a model for the many scholars.]

Associate Examiner, Instructor Xiang 向, comments: [Lofty and ancient insight, grand and imposing talent, and upright and magnanimous sentiment are all fully visible in this piece. title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
若是其異齊茍徒以巍然者寄於上而無所以
治之之具則天下將狃于情之所嚮習之所便
浸淫至于極敝而人君又不能以一人之身殫
精畢力日役役焉爲天下用於是握其機之大
且要者與天下賢士共圖之而吾惟以一心超
然獨運於天下是故君享其逸臣任其勞而無
爲之治成此哲后之上務皇王之大業也昔朱
子論善治在振綱紀然必資宰執之秉持臺諫
之補察而推本於人主以大公至正之心恭巳
===
於上而臨之蓋識體之說也請申其意蓋天爲
民而作之君將以治之安之也顧以天下之大
而民生於其間智者思以儇巧處其利而愚者
亦有所謀勇者思以雄桀重其權而怯者亦有
所逐以至衆寡小大莫不鬨然於好惡之異情
相與競騖而弗巳則民生有欲而各求所以遂
之也夫以民各有必欲遂之私而勢又不可以
自致則不能無求於上求而無度量分界於是
將紛紛籍籍訖無底定而吾旣以身任天下之
punctuated:
若是其異齊，茍徒以巍然者寄於上，而無所以治之之具，則天下將狃于情之所嚮、習之所便，浸淫至于極敝。而人君又不能以一人之身，殫精畢力，日役役焉爲天下用，於是握其機之大且要者，與天下賢士共圖之，而吾惟以一心超然獨運於天下。是故君享其逸，臣任其勞，而無爲之治成。此哲后之上務，皇王之大業也。昔朱子論善治在振綱紀，然必資宰執之秉持、臺諫之補察，而推本於人主以大公至正之心，恭巳於上而臨之，蓋識體之說也。請申其意。
蓋天爲民而作之君，將以治之、安之也。顧以天下之大，而民生於其間，智者思以儇巧處其利，而愚者亦有所謀；勇者思以雄桀重其權，而怯者亦有所逐；以至衆寡、小大，莫不鬨然於好惡之異情，相與競騖而弗巳，則民生有欲，而各求所以遂之也。夫以民各有必欲遂之私，而勢又不可以自致，則不能無求於上；求而無度量分界，於是將紛紛籍籍，訖無底定。而吾旣以身任天下之
translation_en:
…are so varied and uneven. If he merely occupies a lofty position on high without the instruments wherewith to govern it, then the empire will grow habituated to following the inclinations of its passions and the conveniences of its customs, gradually sinking into extreme decay. Yet the ruler of men cannot, in his single person, exhaust his spirit and spend all his strength toiling day after day in the service of the empire. Therefore, he grasps the great and essential pivots of governance and plans them together with the worthy men of the empire, while he himself, with a single mind, transcends above and alone directs the empire. Thus the ruler enjoys his ease, the ministers bear their toil, and governance through non-action is achieved. This is the supreme task of a wise sovereign and the great enterprise of august kings. In the past, Master Zhu [Zhu Xi 朱熹] argued that good governance lies in invigorating the overarching guidelines and regulations, yet it must rely on the firm upholding by the Chief Councilors and Executive Officials and the remonstrance and surveillance by the Censors and Remonstrators, while tracing the root back to the ruler of men, who with a supremely impartial and utterly upright mind reverently composes himself on high and presides over them. This is indeed a doctrine that understands the fundamental body of governance. Allow me to elaborate upon its meaning.

Heaven created a ruler for the people in order to govern them and give them peace. Yet given the vastness of the empire and the people born within it, the clever think of using nimble craft to secure their advantage, while the foolish also have their schemes; the brave think of using fierce prowess to increase their power, while the timid also have what they pursue; and so it goes down to the many and the few, the great and the small—none fail to clamor amid their differing feelings of likes and dislikes, competing and racing with one another without cease. This is because the people are born with desires, and each seeks the means to fulfill them. Now, since the people each have selfish desires that they are determined to fulfill, and yet by circumstance cannot attain them on their own, they cannot avoid making demands upon their superiors. If they make demands and there are no standards of measure or boundaries of station, then things will fall into tumultuous confusion, never reaching settled order. And since I have already taken upon myself the empire's…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
責固不可聽其紛籍而莫爲之所而又不獲人
人而白之以吾志之所欲非操其綱紀以總攝
整齊之何以使之銷意劘私而盡就吾之條理
哉是故善治天下者不視天下之安危察綱紀
之理亂而已夫天下之事未有不由綱紀而理
者綱者猶網之有綱紀者猶絲之有紀綱舉其
大紀張其小也朝廷之綱紀亦多端矣而語其
大且要者則莫如辯賢否以定上下之分核功
罪以公賞罰之施是二者帝王所以維持天下
===
之制繫乎國脈關乎運數而爲天下風俗之所
由成其幾動於至微其變效於至速其秉持補
察在宰執與臺諫而其本在於人主之一心人
主之心何心也大公至正也惟大公乃可以絶
天下之私惟至正乃可以息天下之邪故能爲
天地民物之主百官之表而綱紀之所自出也
夫一家有一家之綱紀一國有一國之綱紀人
主之所振者則天下之綱紀也振天下之綱紀
非以天下之心處之不可而天下之心則大公
punctuated: 責，固不可聽其紛籍而莫爲之所，而又不獲人人而白之以吾志之所欲。非操其綱紀以總攝整齊之，何以使之銷意劘私，而盡就吾之條理哉？是故善治天下者，不視天下之安危，察綱紀之理亂而已。夫天下之事，未有不由綱紀而理者。綱者，猶網之有綱；紀者，猶絲之有紀。綱舉其大，紀張其小也。朝廷之綱紀亦多端矣，而語其大且要者，則莫如辯賢否以定上下之分，核功罪以公賞罰之施。是二者，帝王所以維持天下之制，繫乎國脈，關乎運數，而爲天下風俗之所由成。其幾動於至微，其變效於至速，其秉持補察在宰執與臺諫，而其本在於人主之一心。人主之心，何心也？大公至正也。惟大公，乃可以絶天下之私；惟至正，乃可以息天下之邪。故能爲天地民物之主，百官之表，而綱紀之所自出也。夫一家有一家之綱紀，一國有一國之綱紀，人主之所振者，則天下之綱紀也。振天下之綱紀，非以天下之心處之不可，而天下之心，則大公
translation_en: …responsibility, one certainly cannot allow them to fall into tumultuous disorder without making provision for them, and yet one cannot explain to every single person what one's own will desires. Without grasping the overarching principles and guiding threads (gangji) to gather and regulate them, how could one cause people to dissolve their selfish intentions, wear away their private interests, and conform entirely to one's own orderly pattern? Therefore, those who are skilled at governing the realm do not look at whether the realm is safe or imperiled; they simply examine whether its overarching principles and guiding threads are in order or in disorder. Indeed, among the affairs of the world, there are none that are not put in order through overarching principles and guiding threads. The "headrope" (gang) is like the main cord of a net; the "guiding thread" (ji) is like the sorting thread of silk. The headrope lifts the great; the guiding thread spreads out the small. The overarching principles and guiding threads of the court are also manifold, yet if we speak of what is greatest and most essential among them, nothing surpasses distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy so as to fix the hierarchy of superior and inferior, and verifying merits and offenses so as to make fair the application of rewards and punishments. These two are the institutions by which emperors and kings sustain the realm; they are tied to the lifeblood of the state, bound up with the destiny of the dynasty, and are that from which the customs and mores of the world are formed. Their subtle springs of action stir in the most minute particulars, and their transformations take effect with the greatest speed. Upholding, supplementing, and scrutinizing them rests with the grand councillors and the censors and remonstrators, yet their root lies in the single mind of the ruler. What sort of mind is the mind of the ruler? It is supreme impartiality and utmost rectitude. Only through supreme impartiality can one cut off the selfish interests of the world; only through utmost rectitude can one put an end to the crookedness of the world. Thus he is able to be the lord of Heaven, Earth, the people, and all things, the exemplar for all officials, and the source from which the overarching principles and guiding threads issue forth. Now, a family has the overarching principles and guiding threads of a family, and a state has the overarching principles and guiding threads of a state; what the ruler invigorates is the overarching principles and guiding threads of the entire realm. To invigorate the overarching principles and guiding threads of the realm, it will not do unless one handles them with the mind of the entire realm—and the mind of the entire realm is a mind of supreme impartiality…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
至正之心也蓋嘗觀天下之人至弗齊矣其迪
哲俊乂累行砥名足陟于上者有之寧無奇衺
險側溓涊浮沉可抑之使下乎其鎮撫綏寧鴻
熙勳伐足懋其賞者有之寧無昏墨殘賊淫湎
毀常可威之以刑乎夫人主之心豈不樂天下
之皆賢而鮮不肖皆無罪而有功而勢之所在
固難必責其盡如吾意而勢不能盡如吾意又
甚非吾蕩平正直之道於是立爲綱紀以明示
天下如此而陟如此而黜如此而賞如此而刑
===
待于上者有一定之軌而承于下者有一定之
式使天下皆屈體扶伏以待榮辱生殺於我斯
人主之命常尊而天下之勢統於一攷之周禮
八柄曰爵馭貴祿馭富予馭幸置馭行生馭福
奪馭貧廢馭罪誅馭過是綱紀之所布也而又
有作威作福之權焉有衆共衆棄之典焉蓋威
福之權固人主之所獨攬而必以之與衆則人
主亦不敢以自專也而況爲吾之宰執臺諫乎
坐廟堂而與相可否者宰執也立殿陛而與爭
punctuated: 至正之心也。蓋嘗觀天下之人，至弗齊矣。其迪哲俊乂、累行砥名，足陟于上者有之；寧無奇衺險側、溓涊浮沉，可抑之使下乎？其鎮撫綏寧、鴻熙勳伐，足懋其賞者有之；寧無昏墨殘賊、淫湎毀常，可威之以刑乎？夫人主之心，豈不樂天下之皆賢而鮮不肖、皆無罪而有功？而勢之所在，固難必責其盡如吾意。而勢不能盡如吾意，又甚非吾蕩平正直之道。於是立爲綱紀以明示天下：如此而陟，如此而黜，如此而賞，如此而刑。待于上者有一定之軌，而承于下者有一定之式，使天下皆屈體扶伏，以待榮辱生殺於我，斯人主之命常尊，而天下之勢統於一。攷之《周禮》八柄，曰：爵馭貴、祿馭富、予馭幸、置馭行、生馭福、奪馭貧、廢馭罪、誅馭過，是綱紀之所布也。而又有作威作福之權焉，有衆共衆棄之典焉。蓋威福之權，固人主之所獨攬，而必以之與衆，則人主亦不敢以自專也，而況爲吾之宰執、臺諫乎？坐廟堂而與相可否者，宰執也；立殿陛而與爭
translation_en: … and utterly upright mind. For if one observes the people of the world, they are utterly unequal. There are those who walk in wisdom and are of outstanding talent, who accumulate virtuous deeds and polish their reputations, sufficient to be promoted above; yet how could there not be those who are devious, crooked, treacherous, and biased, who are impure, filthy, and drift with the tide, who should be suppressed and demoted below? There are those who pacify and bring tranquility, whose grand, glorious achievements and merits are sufficient to warrant generous rewards; yet how could there not be those who are benighted, corrupt, cruel, and destructive, who are sunk in debauchery and ruin moral norms, who should be overawed with punishments? Now as for the mind of the ruler of men, how could he not delight in everyone in the world being worthy and few being unworthy, everyone being without crime and possessing merit? Yet given the way circumstances are, it is inherently difficult to insist that everything completely conform to one's wishes. And when circumstances cannot completely conform to one's wishes, and moreover drastically depart from one's broad, impartial, and upright Way, one therefore establishes fundamental principles and regulations to clearly show the world: for such-and-such there is promotion, for such-and-such there is demotion, for such-and-such there is reward, and for such-and-such there is punishment. How those above treat others follows a fixed track, and how those below comply follows a fixed standard. By making the whole world bow their bodies and prostrate themselves to await glory or disgrace, life or death from me, the commands of the ruler of men are ever honored, and the power of the world is unified into one. Examining the Eight Handles of the Rites of Zhou (Zhouli), they are called: rank to control the noble, emolument to control the wealthy, bestowal to control the favored, appointment to control conduct, life to control fortune, deprivation to control the impoverished, dismissal to control the guilty, and censure to control faults—this is how fundamental principles and regulations are promulgated. Moreover, there is the authority toinspiring awe and bestowing blessings, and there is the statute of sharing offices with the multitude and casting out the multitude's despised. For the authority of awe and blessing is indeed monopolized by the ruler of men alone, yet because he must share it with the multitude, even the ruler of men dares not act arbitrarily on his own—how much more so with those who serve as my Grand Councillors and Censors and Remonstrators! Those who sit in the court and deliberate with him on what is acceptable and unacceptable are the Grand Councillors; those who stand at the palace steps and argue with him over…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
是非者臺諫也宰執者政本之重而臺諫則闕
遺之司也故人主爲天下進一賢退一不肖也
宰執曰可臺諫亦曰可然後黜陟行焉黜陟以
宰執以臺諫也吾心無作好作惡也間有異同
吾從而察之而後黜陟之亦此心也爲天下旌
一功罰一罪也宰執曰可臺諫亦曰可然後刑
賞加焉刑賞以宰執以臺諫也吾心無溢喜溢
怒也間有異同吾從而察之而後刑賞之亦此
心也是知綱紀者天下之綱紀宰執可行之臺
===
諫可言之而君心者尤綱紀之綱紀用宰執臺
諫而不有也唯明主獨觀化原既挈天下之綱
紀付之賢宰執又令二三臺諫得言之百司庶
府罔不循令而從事按法而業官而吾心直以
其公平正大者宰之譬之鑑焉烱然無私而天
下之妍媸弗能遁也譬之衡焉戛然不揺而天
下之輕重弗可欺也乃所以握是鑑與衡者匪
惟天下不得而知即人主不得而自知也此豈
以無心忘天下哉恭已於無爲而心運於有爲
punctuated: 是非者，臺諫也。宰執者，政本之重，而臺諫則闕遺之司也。故人主爲天下進一賢、退一不肖也，宰執曰可，臺諫亦曰可，然後黜陟行焉。黜陟以宰執、以臺諫也，吾心無作好作惡也；間有異同，吾從而察之，而後黜陟之，亦此心也。爲天下旌一功、罰一罪也，宰執曰可，臺諫亦曰可，然後刑賞加焉。刑賞以宰執、以臺諫也，吾心無溢喜溢怒也；間有異同，吾從而察之，而後刑賞之，亦此心也。是知綱紀者，天下之綱紀，宰執可行之，臺諫可言之；而君心者，尤綱紀之綱紀，用宰執、臺諫而不有也。唯明主獨觀化原，既挈天下之綱紀付之賢宰執，又令二三臺諫得言之，百司庶府罔不循令而從事、按法而業官，而吾心直以其公平正大者宰之。譬之鑑焉，烱然無私，而天下之妍媸弗能遁也；譬之衡焉，戛然不揺，而天下之輕重弗可欺也。乃所以握是鑑與衡者，匪惟天下不得而知，即人主不得而自知也。此豈以無心忘天下哉？恭已於無爲，而心運於有爲…
translation_en: …over right and wrong are the Censors and Remonstrators. The Grand Councilors carry the weight of the fundamental administration, while the Censors and Remonstrators are the officials in charge of omissions and oversights. Therefore, when the ruler promotes a worthy man or dismisses an unworthy one for the sake of the empire, the Grand Councilors say it is permissible, and the Censors and Remonstrators likewise say it is permissible, and only then are demotions and promotions carried out. Because demotions and promotions are carried out through the Grand Councilors and the Censors and Remonstrators, the ruler's own mind engages in no partiality of fondness or dislike; if occasionally there are differences of opinion among them, he accordingly investigates the matter and only afterward demotes or promotes, which also stems from this same mind. When he honors a merit or punishes a crime for the sake of the empire, the Grand Councilors say it is permissible, and the Censors and Remonstrators likewise say it is permissible, and only then are punishments and rewards applied. Because punishments and rewards are applied through the Grand Councilors and the Censors and Remonstrators, the ruler's own mind indulges in no excessive joy or excessive anger; if occasionally there are differences of opinion among them, he accordingly investigates the matter and only afterward punishes or rewards, which also stems from this same mind. From this we know that the fundamental laws and order are the fundamental laws and order of the empire: the Grand Councilors may implement them, and the Censors and Remonstrators may speak on them; yet the sovereign's mind is even more the governing principle of those fundamental laws and order, employing the Grand Councilors and the Censors and Remonstrators without claiming possession of their functions for himself. Only an enlightened ruler singularly perceives the source of transformation: having entrusted the fundamental laws and order of the empire to worthy Grand Councilors, and having further allowed a few Censors and Remonstrators to speak on them, all the various offices and bureaus without exception follow orders in conducting their affairs and abide by the law in fulfilling their official duties, while the ruler's mind simply governs them through its impartiality, fairness, and uprightness. Compare it to a mirror: it is bright and free of selfishness, so that beauty and ugliness throughout the empire cannot escape it; compare it to a balance scale: it stands firm and unshakable, so that weight and lightness throughout the empire cannot deceive it. Yet the means by which he holds this mirror and balance scale is something that not only the empire cannot know, but even the ruler himself cannot consciously know. How could this mean forgetting the empire through having an empty mind? He maintains reverent self-restraint in non-action, while his mind operates within active governance…

title: 萬曆柒年應天府鄉試錄
text:
也夫人主一心而天下則億萬心也天下雖億
萬心而賢之欲陟否之欲黜功之欲賞罪之欲
刑則億萬者皆同是心也人主不自役其智力
於天下而惟以天下之所同欲者經緯於虛明
空湛之中以求當乎天下之人之心是以端冕
凝旒於南面目不煩視耳不煩聽手不煩揮而
能使天下之人無不慓而悟趯而趨爭相勸勉
奮厲思所以去惡而從善蘄得吾之陟與賞而
不至爲黜罰之所加是故綱維立而衆赴之如
===
流水風行而天下承之疾若偃草則以運之心
者神也噫此人主之所以恭已也自昔帝王稱
盛治者莫如堯舜觀其九德之采四凶之誅元
凱之舉渾沌三族之去蓋惟聽舜禹皐陶爲之
而獨以其兢業之懷允恭溫恭之度日臨于上
而未嘗自用其勞故曰垂衣裳而天下治者此
也後世非不欲振綱紀以維持天下然或闇於
體要之崇而悅乎煩苛之習忽於倚毗之任而
信乎耳目之專乃其意固與聖人遠矣又奚怪
punctuated:
也。夫人主一心，而天下則億萬心也。天下雖億萬心，而賢之欲陟、否之欲黜、功之欲賞、罪之欲刑，則億萬者皆同是心也。人主不自役其智力於天下，而惟以天下之所同欲者，經緯於虛明空湛之中，以求當乎天下之人之心。是以端冕凝旒於南面，目不煩視、耳不煩聽、手不煩揮，而能使天下之人無不慓而悟、趯而趨，爭相勸勉奮厲，思所以去惡而從善，蘄得吾之陟與賞，而不至爲黜罰之所加。是故綱維立而衆赴之如流水，風行而天下承之疾若偃草，則以運之心者神也。噫！此人主之所以恭已也。

自昔帝王稱盛治者，莫如堯、舜。觀其九德之采、四凶之誅、元凱之舉、渾沌三族之去，蓋惟聽舜、禹、皐陶爲之，而獨以其兢業之懷、允恭溫恭之度日臨于上，而未嘗自用其勞。故曰「垂衣裳而天下治」者，此也。後世非不欲振綱紀以維持天下，然或闇於體要之崇，而悅乎煩苛之習；忽於倚毗之任，而信乎耳目之專。乃其意固與聖人遠矣，又奚怪
translation_en:
… Now, the ruler has a single mind, whereas the realm has hundreds of millions of minds. Although the realm has hundreds of millions of minds, in desiring that the worthy be promoted, the unworthy be demoted, merit be rewarded, and crime be punished, those hundreds of millions all share this same mind. The ruler does not personally exhaust his own wisdom and strength upon the realm, but simply takes what the entire realm jointly desires and weaves it together within the empty brightness and clear stillness of his mind, seeking to match the minds of the people of the realm. Therefore, sitting facing south with his ceremonial crown upright and its pendant strings still, his eyes do not trouble to look, his ears do not trouble to listen, and his hands do not trouble to wave, yet he is able to cause everyone in the realm without exception to be startled into awareness and leap to hasten forward, vying to encourage and rouse one another, pondering how to cast off evil and follow the good, hoping to obtain our promotion and reward and not come to have demotion and punishment inflicted upon them. For this reason, when the overarching principles of order are established, the multitude flocks to them like flowing water; when his moral influence moves like the wind, the realm responds to it as swiftly as grass bending before it. This is because that which operates within his mind is marvelous. Ah! This is how the ruler maintains reverent self-composure.

Since antiquity, among emperors and kings praised for flourishing governance, none equaled Yao 堯 and Shun 舜. Observing their selection of the Nine Virtues, the execution of the Four Fiends, the elevation of the "Eight Worthies" (Ba Yuan 八元) and "Eight Harmonies" (Ba Kai 八凱), and the banishment of the three clans of Hundun 渾沌 and others—in truth Yao simply let Shun, Yu 禹, and Gao Yao 皐陶 carry these out, while he alone, with an attitude of cautious diligence and a demeanor of sincere and gentle reverence, presided daily from above without ever personally expending his own toil. Thus, when it is said, "They let their robes hang down and the realm was governed," this is what is meant.
